What I work on

How plants share pollinators, and what this means for the pollen that reaches their stigmas



Sweden connection

SCAPE meetings since 2018, including Höör 2019



Keep this short, about one minute. Botanist by training, working on pollination since the bachelor’s thesis. PhD thesis: factors influencing pollen carryover effectiveness (cum laude, 2024). Current project (GAČR Postdoc Individual Fellowship Outgoing, 25-17193O): long-term spatiotemporal dynamics in a plant–pollinator community and consequences for pollen transfer in a changing world. That project is what this talk is about.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text: [0:30] Let the meadow speak. Handrkov in August: dozens of plant species in flower at the same time, hundreds of insect species.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
What is pollination?
≈ 1 min




Pollen is producedin the anthers



›




An animal carries itto another flower



›




It must land on a stigmaof the same species




→ fertilisation → seeds


For the non-specialists: plants cannot move, so to mate they need a courier. Pollen from one flower has to reach the stigma of another flower of the same species. Pollen landing on the wrong species is lost, and can even block the stigma. The three photos are from our meadow: Succisa anther, a hoverfly (Eristalis interruptus) covered in pollen, a Succisa stigma.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Why does it matter?
≈ 1.5 min



≈ 88 %


of flowering plants are pollinated by animals


Ollerton, Winfree, and Tarrant (2011)




75 %


of leading crop types benefit from animal pollination


Klein et al. (2007)




5–8 %


of global crop production, US$ 235–577 billion per year


Potts et al. (2016)





Pollinators are declining, and most pollination happensin diverse communities where plants share their pollinators.



Ollerton et al. 2011: about 87.5 % of flowering plant species are animal-pollinated (higher in the tropics, about 78 % in temperate communities). Klein et al. 2007: 87 of 115 leading global food crops (75 %) benefit from animal pollination. Potts et al. 2016 (IPBES assessment): 5–8 % of global crop production is directly attributable to animal pollination, worth US$ 235–577 billion per year. Decline: e.g. Hallmann et al. 2017 found a more than 75 % drop in flying insect biomass over 27 years in German protected areas. Bridge: pollination is not one plant and one bee. In a meadow like ours, dozens of plants share the same insects. That is the starting point of our work.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Sharing is the norm
≈ 1.5 min


















Not only bees: in our meadow hoverflies, flies, beetles, butterflies and moths all visit flowers (photos: burnet moth on Sanguisorba, Eristalis on Achillea, butterflies on Succisa). In species-rich meadows most plants are generalists and share most of their visitors. Sharing is a problem for a plant: pollen is lost to other species (consumption, wrong stigmas) and foreign pollen arrives on its own stigma (heterospecific pollen, HP). Central question of the whole talk: how do plants in such a meadow still get enough of their own pollen (conspecific pollen, CP)?

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
The locality
≈ 1 min




Czech Republic





> 50 entomophilous plant species




15 years of data collection (2011–2025)


Study design: Janovský et al. (2013)


K Handrkovu near Vernýřov, Central Bohemia (49.8466 N, 15.1498 E). Moist to mesophilous grassland mosaic, two flowering peaks (May, August), mown twice a year. Sampling at the August peak. Where it started: Janovský et al. 2013 (PLoS ONE) set up the plot design and showed that conspecific and heterospecific flower densities at a scale of a few metres drive which pollinators visit a plant. This small-scale density effect comes back twice in this talk: dilution of foreign pollen on Succisa stigmas (Part 3) and the pull of the core species (Part 4).

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Why should timing matter?
≈ 1 min


Only a tiny fraction of pollen reaches a conspecific stigma
Pollen presentation theory: plants can dose pollen to pollinators (Harder and Thomson 1989)
With shared pollinators, when pollen is offered may decide who carries it



Optional: add Harder & Wilson 1994, LeBuhn & Holsinger 1998 and Stone et al. 1998 to techroom/references.bib (from Psani_clanku/2021/START_paper/pollen_presentation_references.bib).


Pollen is lost through consumption, grooming and transfer to the wrong species. Gradual dispensing should pay off with many, inefficient pollinators; dumping all pollen at once should pay off with few, efficient ones.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Three species, three strategies
≈ 1 min


 

Succisa pratensis


Open flowers, pollen freely exposedMainly pollen-feeding hoverflies



 

Centaurea jacea


Pollen pumped out of the anther tubeMainly bees



 

Trifolium hybridum


Closed flowers, pollen released when a bee opens themBees only




Photos: Lukáš Janošík · Štenc et al. (2023)


Three co-flowering species at Handrkov that share part of their pollinators but differ in how pollen is presented. Click: close-ups of pollen presentation. Succisa: anthers fully exposed, pollen easy to take. Centaurea: Asteraceae pump mechanism, the style pushes pollen out of the anther tube gradually. Trifolium: pollen hidden in the keel, released only when a bee forces the flower open. Colours of the species names match the curves on the next slides.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
How we measured pollen release
≈ 0.5 min










Every hour, 8:00–17:00, two days
Flowers offering pollen from 5 inflorescences per species → vial with stained detergent solution
Pollen grains in each vial counted
Flowers offering pollen counted on 20 inflorescences



→ pollen available per inflorescence, hour by hour



Photo: Lukáš Janošík · Štenc et al. (2023)


START I methods (Štenc et al. 2023, AJB): 15 and 16 August 2021, hourly sampling, 5 vials per species per hour, each vial = flowers from 5 random inflorescences (3 flowers for Trifolium and Centaurea, 5 for Succisa) in 2 ml of detergent with basic fuchsin. Only flowers actively presenting pollen and visited by pollinators were taken. Pollinator visitation was recorded in parallel, so pollen supply and visits can be compared hour by hour.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Swabbing pollinators
≈ 1 min










Catch the insect on the flower, swab one half of the body
Cube of glycerine jelly with fuchsin picks up the pollen
Melt the jelly on a slide
Count every second square, identify 200 grains



Result per insect: load (grains) and purity (share of own pollen)



Beattie (1971) · figure from Freudenfeld et al. (2025)


Same protocol in START II, in Freudenfeld et al. 2025 and in the deposition paper (body loads on Succisa visitors). Bees: pollen packed in the corbiculae is not swabbed, because it no longer takes part in pollination. Counts therefore refer to one quarter of the body (half the body swabbed, half of the squares counted). Conspecific = pollen of the plant on which the insect was caught. Heterospecific = everything else.

What do pollinators carry?
≈ 1.5 min








Štenc et al. (2025)




Succisa: most pollen in the morning, then quantity and purity drop
Centaurea, Trifolium: more even loads through the day
Explained by plant density (Centaurea) and flower morphology with release strategy (Trifolium)




Štenc et al. 2025, PPEES 67: 125868. Conspecific pollen on pollinator bodies over the day (log scale), by pollinator taxon.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Pollen must flow
≈ 1 min






Štenc et al. (2025)


Pollinator performance = visitation activity per flowering stalk × conspecific pollen grains on the body. Succisa is served by hoverflies early in the morning (Eristalis tenax, Helophilus), Centaurea and Trifolium by Apis in the afternoon. The plants split the day: diurnal stratification of pollen transfer lowers the cost of sharing pollinators.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Who carries the pollen?
≈ 1 min













618 pollinators, 2020–2021, Handrkov · Freudenfeld et al. (2025)


Bridge from the three focal plants: now the whole pollinator community. Pollen swabbed with fuchsin jelly from one half of the body; counts are per quarter of the body. Step 1: every dot is one insect. Loads range from a few grains to thousands within the same group. Step 2 (click): group means with 95 % CI. Groups do differ (ANOVA F(30, 531) = 21.3, p < 0.001, 54.6 % of variance), bees and large Eristalis carry most, Pieris and Coenonympha least. But most groups overlap broadly: the spread among individuals is as large as the spread among groups. Figure redrawn from raw data (35 groups); the paper’s model used 31 groups.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Who visits changes every year
≈ 1 min













45 472 visits, 2011–2021 · Freudenfeld et al. (2025)


Step 1: interaction density of each pollinator group per year (32 groups, grey lines). Step 2 (click): the most abundant groups. Sarcophagidae, Apis and Sphaerophoria jump several-fold between consecutive years. Eristalis tenax is the most constant of the dominant groups.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Abundance, not identity
≈ 0.5 min






Coefficient of variation = SD / mean, i.e. spread relative to the average


Data: Freudenfeld et al. (2025)



Pollinators differ little in how much pollen they carry.Their contribution is set by how abundant they are that year.



Coefficients of variation: among group means of pollen load (0.75), median within-group CV of pollen load among individuals (0.77), median CV of visitation density among years within a group (1.13). Values computed for this slide from the paper’s data (scripts/fig_freudenfeld_2025.R). Conclusion of Freudenfeld et al. 2025: a pollinator’s contribution to pollen transfer depends more on its abundance than on its capacity to carry pollen. A diverse pollinator community buffers the decline of any single taxon. Bridge to Part 3: if many different, variable carriers deliver pollen, what finally arrives on the stigma?

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Preference and constancy
≈ 1 min








Interview stick: offer two flowers, record which one the insect chooses next









Preference: which flower is chosen more often than expected
Constancy: staying on the same species in consecutive visits, more than preference alone predicts




Two different behaviours that are often mixed up. Preference = choosing one flower type over another. Constancy = repeating the previous choice. A constant pollinator carries purer loads, so constancy matters directly for heterospecific pollen. Interview stick (Thomson 1981): a stick carrying two flowers is offered to a foraging insect; the choice relative to the flower it just left is recorded. Arrays of real or artificial flowers do the same with many flowers at once. The transition matrix shows how often an insect moves from each species to each other species; constancy is the excess on the diagonal.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
How do pollinators choose?
≈ 1 min


3D-printed flowers, 3 % sucrose, Eristalis tenax · Matoušková, Štenc, and Janovský (2023); Haveldová et al. (submitted)


Bridge: the field tells us who visits. To see how an individual pollinator decides, we went to the lab. A: arena with two flower forms in a chessboard pattern, 15 cm apart, so the fly must fly between flowers. B: each flight is scored as constant (same form) or switching. C: four forms, yellow or white, large or small. D: in the field E. tenax visits mostly Succisa. E: in the fly’s colour space, the white form sits next to Succisa, Centaurea and Selinum, the yellow form next to Leontodon. So the artificial flowers mimic real core plants of the meadow. Matoušková et al. 2023 (Biol. J. Linn. Soc.): naive E. tenax select colour most strongly, then size, symmetry only weakly; yellow is preferred, especially when large.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Experience changes the choice
≈ 1 min










Naive flies (lab-reared): strong innate preference for yellow




Experienced flies (caught in the meadow): no colour preference left
Flower constancy 10–15 % lower after experience




5 270 visits by naive and 31 973 by experienced flies · Haveldová, Štenc, Matoušková & Janovský (submitted)


Share of all visits that went to yellow forms, summed over the four forms (naive: YL 1 829 + YS 1 682 of 4 841 visits; experienced: 8 000 + 7 855 of 31 973). Caveat: visits were not spread evenly across treatments, so this is a summary of the raw counts, not the model. The GLMs show significant colour, size and interaction effects in both groups (Table 1 of the manuscript). Experienced flies from a flower-rich meadow are more opportunistic: weaker preferences and lower constancy. They also reacted more to which flowers they could see from their position (angular area ratio). Implication for the plant: an experienced hoverfly arriving on Succisa has likely just visited something else.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Who stays faithful?
≈ 1 min







Hoverflies, the main visitors of Succisa,are among the least constant pollinators.



Literature synthesis + our field experiments, 20 sources, experimental data only · Sedláčková, Štenc, Matoušková & Janovský (in prep.)


Share of foraging decisions explained by flower constancy, from interview-stick and array experiments (quasibinomial GLM, F = 15.8, p < 0.001). Honeybees and other bees about 0.75–0.80; bumblebees, butterflies and hoverflies 0.22–0.34. Points = individual studies or species pairs. Bridge to Part 3: a meadow served by inconstant hoverflies should load stigmas with foreign pollen. So what actually lands on a Succisa stigma? Manuscript is an early draft; numbers may change.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Part 2 in one sentence
≈ 0.5 min


Plants cannot choose their pollinators,but they can choose when to offer pollen.Who carries it, and how faithfully, changes with the year and with experience.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
From body to stigma
≈ 1 min




Pollen on the body





Pollen on the stigma




Define terms once: conspecific pollen (CP) = own species; heterospecific pollen (HP) = other species. Single-visit deposition (SVD) = what one visit leaves. Terminal pollen deposition (TPD) = the final load on an old stigma. Focal species from now on: Succisa pratensis, a core species of the meadow network (Part 4).

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Defining the deposition steps
≈ 1 min



1. Pollinator Body Load





CP (Conspecific)





HP (Heterospecific)




Pollen carried by visitor.Can be own species (CP) or foreign (HP).




2. Single Visit (SVD)





Pollen left by one visit on virgin stigma.Mechanically inefficient & noisy (high CV).




3. Terminal Load (TPD)





Final cumulative load on old stigma.Accumulated visits buffer noise (low CV).




Define terms explicitly: - CP = Conspecific Pollen (own species) - HP = Heterospecific Pollen (foreign pollen from neighbours) - SVD = Single-Visit Deposition: measured experimentally with virgin bagged stigmas exposed to exactly 1 visit. - TPD = Terminal Pollen Deposition: the final load on naturally pollinated stigmas.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
How we measure deposition
≈ 1 min



Single visit (SVD)



Bag the inflorescence in tulle before anthers open
Unbag when stigmas are receptive
Wait for one visit, note the visitor
Collect the visited stigma into ethanol






Replace with a photo of a bagged Succisa inflorescence, if you have one.




Terminal load (TPD)



Flowers with withered corolla = end of stigma life
3 stigmas per head, 30 plants per day
Clear, stain with safranin, squash
Count own and foreign grains at 400×



 




SVD: 124 controlled single visits on virgin stigmas, 2022–2024. If the insect visited more than one flower, only the first stigma was kept. TPD: 693 terminal-stage stigmas from 273 plants, 2022–2024. Slide preparation: 10 % KOH, 3 % H2O2, 8 % acetic acid, then safranin–glycerol, squash under a coverslip, seal with nail polish. Micrograph: Succisa stigma with large own pollen grains and smaller foreign grains. Own and foreign grains are told apart by size, shape and surface ornamentation. The Slavkovský les stigmas were processed the same way.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
One visit is a lottery
≈ 1.5 min






One visit leaves only ≈ 2 % of the body’s own pollen on the stigma · no difference among Eristalis, Helophilus and Bombus


SVD experiments 2022–2024 on bagged Succisa inflorescences (124 single visits; 300 pollinators swabbed for body loads). Mean body load: CP 148 grains (SD 394), HP 479 (SD 1 102). Only about 2.3 % of body CP and 0.1 % of body HP end up on the stigma in one visit. Kruskal–Wallis among dominant morphogroups: CP H3 = 1.59, p = 0.66; HP H3 = 5.20, p = 0.16. Per visit, the pollinators are functionally equivalent, which fits the Freudenfeld result: what matters is how many visits, not who makes them.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
section: But the final load is stable
text:
But the final load is stable
≈ 1.5 min













CV of conspecific pollen: body 129 % → single visit 206 % → terminal load 69 %. Heterospecific pollen stays variable: body 264 % → terminal 147 %. Variance partitioning of TPD (693 stigmas, 273 plants, 2022–2024): years and days explain little CP variance; plants 15 %, stigmas 82 %. Within 2024, days were not significant (CP χ² = 1.32, p = 0.52). HP is different: year (χ² = 32.4, p < 0.001) and plant (χ² = 104.7, p < 0.001) both matter.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
The law of large numbers
≈ 1.5 min













Monte Carlo simulation parameterised by empirical SVD and visitation rates: accumulation of many independent, noisy visits is sufficient to reproduce the stable terminal CP loads observed in the field. HP is different: not predicted by the null model, depends on the floral neighbourhood, and is diluted by high conspecific floral density. Štenc et al., submitted to New Phytologist.

From one meadow to a landscape
≈ 1 min






Slavkovský les Protected Landscape Area, W Bohemia · land cover ESA WorldCover 2021 · relief AWS Terrain Tiles · boundary © OpenStreetMap


Handrkov is one meadow followed for three years. Slavkovský les asks the same question across a landscape: 60 Succisa meadows in a mosaic of forest, pasture, wetland margins and ponds. Each meadow sampled once: 37 in 2022, 23 in 2023. Field work: MSc thesis of Natálie Hanusová (2024), supervised by J. Štenc.

≈ 1 min



photo Natálie HanusováMSc thesis 2024 · field work, pollen counts



60 meadows, one sampling day each


1 035 plants · 3 065 stigmas3 stigmas per plant, ≈ 20 plants per meadow


4 595 visitors, 81 taxa20-min transects, morning and afternoon

Same protocol as Handrkov: male-phase flowers, three stigmas per plant, conspecific (CP) and heterospecific (HP) grains counted. Plants per meadow: median 20 (range 7–21). Spread of meadow means (10th–90th percentile): CP 2.2×, HP 8.0×; CV 0.33 vs 0.85.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
section: Buffered in time and in space
text:
Buffered in time and in space
≈ 2 min






Own pollen: little variance between years (3 %) or meadows (11 %). Foreign pollen: about a third (34 % and 30 %).


The same model on both datasets: linear mixed model on sqrt counts, plant nested in year (Handrkov) or in meadow (Slavkovský les), stigma = residual. CP: the big share is plant and stigma, i.e. local and chance. Neither years nor meadows matter much. That is what the law of large numbers predicts. HP: about a third sits at the year or meadow level. Foreign pollen depends on context. The Bayesian Poisson model in the manuscript gives the same picture (CP meadow 13 %, HP 43 %).

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Foreign pollen follows the neighbours
≈ 1.5 min







More Succisa flowerheads → less HP (dilution, as at Handrkov)
Wetter surroundings (marsh, close to water) → more HP
Landscape explains 35 % of HP between meadows, only 12 % of CP
Visitor composition explains neither



Meadow-level RDA on mean HP: flowerheads F = 21.5, p = 0.001; distance to water F = 7.9, p = 0.008; marsh area F = 5.1, p = 0.023; adj. R² = 0.35. CP: only meadow area (positive), adj. R² = 0.12. Dilution: Spearman ρ = −0.50 between flowerhead number and HP. Large Succisa populations keep visitors on Succisa. Visitor community (dbRDA, n = 58 meadows): CP adj. R² 0.007, p = 0.38; HP 0.022, p = 0.30.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Taller plants get more pollen
≈ 1 min






But traits leave plant-to-plant variance unchanged (ICC 0.793 → 0.794)


Optional: photo of a tall Succisa above the grass.


Within a meadow, plants taller than their neighbours get about 11 % more conspecific pollen per SD of height (RR 1.11, 1.04–1.19). Height does not affect HP. Larger flowerheads collect slightly more HP (RR 1.10). Height shifts the mean. Most plant-to-plant variation remains position, microhabitat or chance.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Is taller better?
≈ 1 min



photo Klára Hodánkovárole / affiliation


photo Javier Valverderole / affiliation



Field work 2026





Taller flowers stick out of the grass and receive more own pollen (Slavkovský les). But does more pollen also mean better pollen?




Fill in species, site and sampling date (the data files do not say; I assumed Succisa pratensis), roles and affiliations. Add the two photos when you have them.


Introduce the people first: this was the 2026 field season with Klára Hodánková and Javier Valverde. Starting point: Slavkovský les showed that within a meadow, taller plants receive more own pollen. Height makes a flower more visible and easier to reach for flying insects. The new question: is all that extra pollen equally useful?

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
section: From pollen grain to pollen tube
text:
From pollen grain to pollen tube
≈ 1 min









Pollen lands on the stigma




A compatible grain germinates: a tube grows down the style to the ovule
Only grains with a tube can fertilise



What we measured Height of every flowering stalk (194 stalks, 100 plants) Pollen grains and pollen tubes on 61 stigmas from 32 plants



Add how stigmas were stained for tubes (e.g. aniline blue under fluorescence) and when they were collected.


Pollen tubes are the step between deposition and fertilisation. Counting tubes per stigma tells us how much of the deposited pollen actually germinated. Two stigmas (flowers A and B) per plant; random effects for plant and flower in all models.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Height, pollen and pollen tubes
≈ 2 min








Most plants are 25–40 cm tall · only 3 % of stalks exceed 50 cm


Pollen per stigma rises with height and levels off at ≈ 50 cm · grey bars = plant heights in the meadow


Pollen tubes follow a flatter curve, peaking at ≈ 45 cm


The share of grains with a tube falls: ≈ 45 % at 15 cm → ≈ 24 % at 65 cm



2026 · with Klára Hodánková and Javier Valverde · unpublished


Step 1: context. Height of 194 flowering stalks on 100 plants, median 32 cm; about 60 % are 25–40 cm, only 3 % above 50 cm. So most plants sit on the rising part of the next curve. Step 2: own pollen per stigma ~ quadratic height, negative binomial GLMM with plant/flower random effects: linear z = 4.2, p < 0.001; quadratic z = −3.6, p < 0.001; predicted peak at about 50 cm. The tall end rests on few plants. Step 3: number of pollen tubes ~ quadratic height (Poisson GLMM): linear p = 0.32, quadratic p = 0.014, peak at about 45 cm. No confidence band shown for this curve; the model’s interval is not informative. Step 4: proportion of grains with a tube ~ height (binomial GLMM): β = −0.019 per cm, p = 0.041. Take-home: taller plants get more pollen, but a smaller share of it germinates. Possible reasons: more self or related pollen from long visits on tall plants, competition among grains, or older stigmas. One season, one site: a lead to follow, not a result.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
section: Pollen deposition through a flower’s life
text:
Pollen deposition through a flower’s life
≈ 2 min













Redraw the GAMM figure: the confidence bands are broken and “Unknown” / “SC” add noise. Show SI vs SIC only. Literature synthesis: 36 species, 23 families, 49 surveys, 194 time-stamped records.


Meta-analysis of published deposition time series (Štenc, in prep.). Mating system best predicts the curve shape (deviance explained 56.8 %). Self-incompatible species accumulate pollen over a broader part of flower life (median AUC 0.72 vs 0.14 in SIC; p_adj = 0.024) but rarely reach P/O ≥ 1 (1 of 7 surveys). Long accumulation without saturation: a sign of chronic pollen limitation in obligate outcrossers. Bridge back to Succisa: protandrous, long-lived stigmas, hence the value of many visits.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
How it fits together
≈ 1 min



Anther


Time


Pollen release schedules split the day among co-flowering plants



›



Pollinator


Who & how


Abundance sets who carries pollen; experience lowers constancy



›



Stigma


Numbers


Many noisy visits give a stable dose of own pollen



›



Neighbourhood


Space


Foreign pollen follows the neighbours and the landscape





Own pollen is secured by many visits.Foreign pollen is decided by the community.



One sentence per step, each backed by one study from Parts 2 and 3. The last step is the bridge: if foreign pollen depends on the neighbours, we need to understand the whole community of neighbours. That is the pollinator-sharing network.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Plants linked by shared pollinators
≈ 1 min













From the bipartite plant-pollinator web to the plant-plant pollinator-sharing network. Every shared visitor is a potential route for HP. Shortened version of the SCAPE 2026 story. If time allows, reuse the airport analogy slide from SCAPE.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
What is the core?
≈ 1 min



Photo: Colin, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0






All plants






Peel weakly linked plants






What remains = core





k-core decomposition (Seidman 1983), done separately for each year. Think of an onion: remove plants with few sharing links, repeat until only a mutually connected centre remains. A species counts as core if it is central more often than expected from its flower abundance (null model, 1 000 permutations per year).

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
A stable core
≈ 1.5 min






k-core decomposition per year, null model of 1 000 permutations per year. Six species are central in the sharing network across 15 years: Centaurea jacea, Selinum carvifolia, Succisa pratensis, Pimpinella saxifraga, Achillea ptarmica, Ranunculus acris. Plant identity explains 38 % of centrality variance beyond floral abundance (44 %). Note that the two best-studied species of Parts 2 and 3, Succisa and Centaurea, are both core species.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026

Recurring summer drought
≈ 0.5 min






Data: TerraClimate (Abatzoglou et al. 2018), Handrkov locality (2011–2025)


Recurring summer drought in 2011–2025. Only 2013 and 2021 were wet summers; 2018 was the driest, followed by 2015, 2019 and 2025.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
section: Drought concentrates visits on the core
text:
Drought concentrates visits on the core
≈ 1.5 min













Step 1: share of all visits going to the 6 core species, rising from 34–55 % (2011–14) to 84–88 % (2023–25). Step 2 (click): share of flowers produced by the core. On average the core holds about 14 % of flowers but receives 67 % of visits. In dry years peripheral flowering drops about threefold, core flowering does not.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
How robust is the network?
≈ 1 min















Co-extinction simulation following Memmott, Waser, and Price (2004)


Remove plants one by one and count how many pollinators lose all their food plants. Robustness R = area under the curve: 1 = nothing is lost, 0 = immediate collapse. Click 1: removing peripheral plants first, the curve stays high (R ≈ 0.85). Click 2: removing core plants first, pollinators are lost quickly (R ≈ 0.45). Next slide: how this changes across 15 years.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
A more fragile network
≈ 1.5 min






Co-extinction simulation following Memmott, Waser, and Price (2004)



Losing the core costs more in dry years and more every year



Co-extinction simulations (Memmott et al. 2004). Core-first removal: R from 0.69 (2011) to 0.41–0.43 (2023–25). Robustness gap grows by about 0.022 per year. Link to pollen: if most visits go to a few core plants, those plants share almost every insect. What does that mean for the pollen arriving on their stigmas? That is the open question of Part 5.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Visits are not pollen
≈ 1.5 min























Concept, not data. Pollen-transfer networks built from stigma loads and body loads, compared to visitation networks. Does pollen actually flow along the same routes, in the same direction and strength?

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
section: The price of being in the core
text:
The price of being in the core
≈ 1.5 min









Hypothesis: when drought crowds pollinators onto the core, core plants share almost every insect and receive more foreign pollen.


First hint on Succisa stigmas: own pollen stable, foreign pollen highest in dry 2023, lowest in 2024 when Succisa flowered densely.



Three years cannot separate drought from Succisa density. Say so, and present this as the motivation for continued stigma sampling (SucTemDep) and the apparent-competition project.


Mean grains per terminal-stage stigma (± SE): CP 20.5, 20.5, 27.4; HP 35.2, 50.4, 9.6 for 2022, 2023, 2024 (84, 89 and 520 stigmas). Summer drought index: 2022 mild, 2023 dry, 2024 moderate. In 2024 Succisa flowered much more densely, and the Monte Carlo model shows HP dropping towards the mechanical baseline. So density dilution is the better-supported explanation; drought is a hypothesis to test. Apparent competition bottleneck project (pitch stage): core species sharing most visits may pay a cost in foreign pollen, which could be one reason they do not exclude the periphery.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
section: Time of day as a niche axis
text:
Time of day as a niche axis
≈ 1 min

Project DiuHanPolNet (manuscript draft). Diurnal stratification structures the network: “global generalists, local specialists”.

Hourly interaction rewiring ≈ 34 %
Diurnal stratification reduces apparent competition by > 40 % per year
Pollinators shift foraging time away from dominant competitors (Apis, dominant Diptera)

This scales Part 2 (three species) to the whole community. Decide whether the harmonogram below reads well at slide size.

section: From pollen on the stigma to seeds
text:
From pollen on the stigma to seeds
≈ 1 min



Pollen deposited


what we measure now



›



Pollen tubes


first data in 2026



›



Seeds


next step





Does a stable dose of own pollen mean stable seed set?
Does foreign pollen reduce tube growth, especially in dry years?
Is quality, not quantity, the limit for tall, well-visited plants?




Do you have data on stigma pollen loads, pollen tubes or seed set?We would love to combine them.



Future direction: follow pollen one step further, from deposition to germination and seeds. Planned: pollen tubes and seed set on Succisa across years at Handrkov, linked to the yearly foreign-pollen loads and drought. Call for data: datasets with stigma loads plus pollen tubes or seed set, from any species, would let us test whether the law-of-large-numbers buffering of deposition carries through to fertilisation. We are also collecting published time series of pollen deposition (the deposition-curve synthesis).

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
section: Backup: does more pollen mean more seeds?
text:
Backup: does more pollen mean more seeds?

Expected question. No seed set data yet; the closest is the 2026 pollen-tube data (see the height slide). Prepare a spoken answer: Succisa has one ovule per flower, so a terminal load of ≈ 20–27 conspecific grains is far above the minimum; the open question is whether foreign pollen (up to ≈ 50 grains in 2023) clogs stigmas enough to reduce seed set. If you have any seed set or pollen-tube data, put one figure here.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Backup: pollen production per inflorescence






START I data: Succisa produces roughly an order of magnitude less pollen per inflorescence than Centaurea or Trifolium (≈ 0.4 × 10⁵ vs 2.6–3.5 × 10⁵), and releases it all in the morning.
